abstract: Geopolitical tensions are changing the nature of supply-chain risk. This column presents new survey evidence showing that EU firms increasingly regard trade disruptions as persistent but are moving away from emergency responses such as stockpiling towards longer-term diversification of suppliers and markets. The EU Single Market provides an important buffer against external shocks. At the same time, experimental evidence shows that geopolitical disruptions can have sizeable and asymmetric effects on firms' investment.
authors: Marine Charlotte André, Román Arjona, Enrique Feás, Péter Harasztosi, Laurent Maurin, Frank Vandermeeren, Xosé-Luís Varela-Irimia, Christoph Weiss

abstract: The human and economic costs of extreme weather events are already large and will grow as temperatures rise further. This column argues that, seen through the lens of the sovereign balance sheet rather than the budget, adaptation reduces the expected fiscal cost of physical climate risk – and the case for investing in it becomes clear.

abstract: The theory of optimal currency hedging has been well established for decades. This column uses new regulatory data to analyse how 2,806 European investment funds use currency forwards and swaps and how the use compares to theoretical benchmarks. It finds that only a minority follow hedging policies close to the portfolio-theory benchmark, and observed derivative trading does not significantly contribute to lower fund risk. Yet a feasible optimal strategy could lower volatility by about 10%, at very modest additional transaction cost.
title: European funds often fall short on currency hedging

abstract: Residential photovoltaic (PV) adoption changes both household electricity use and its sources, but post-adoption dynamics remain less understood. Using monthly panel data on 21,320 households in Tianjin, China, from 2019 to 2024, including 6320 PV adopters and 15,000 never-adopting households, this study examines changes in total electricity consumption and grid-purchased electricity following PV adoption. A difference-in-differences design with household and year-month fixed effects shows that PV adoption is associated with a 5.4% increase in total electricity consumption and a 75.2% reduction in grid-purchased electricity. An accounting decomposition indicates that 82.3% of the reduction in grid-purchased electricity reflects substitution by self-generated PV electricity, while 17.7% corresponds to increased total consumption. The increase in consumption is concentrated in the earlier post-adoption period and gradually attenuates over time, whereas the reduction in grid-purchased electricity becomes larger. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing changes in electricity sources from changes in household electricity use when evaluating residential PV deployment.

abstract: In the absence of bureaucratic autonomy, environmental regulations may become institutional traps: rules designed to protect the environment that instead institutionalize environmental injustice. This paper examines this proposition through the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) system in Peru’s large-scale mining sector. Drawing on administrative records and interviews with public and private EIA actors, it traces the institutional evolution of EIAs since their introduction in the early 1990s and analyzes the development—and limits—of bureaucratic autonomy in environmental governance. Environmental regulation has consistently faced resistance from extractivist interests, with major reforms emerging only through contingent windows of opportunity. Against a backdrop of low state autonomy, we identify two periods in the political differentiation of the EIA system from the regulated industry: (1) the 1990s–2010s, when the Ministry of Energy and Mines retained responsibility for EIA certification, limiting regulatory independence; and (2) the 2010s–2020s, marked by the creation of SENACE, followed by renewed deregulation aimed at making environmental governance more responsive to extractive interests. Although SENACE’s autonomy remains constrained, it has strengthened technical capacity and legitimacy within technopolitical networks. The case identifies three conditions under which EIA systems become institutional traps: structural dependence on extractive rents, regulators lacking political differentiation and financial autonomy, and weakened expert and civil society networks. Where these conditions converge, formal environmental rules function primarily as instruments of legitimation, making bureaucratic autonomy a necessary, though not sufficient, condition for substantive environmental protection.
title: Rules without autonomy: environmental impact assessment as an institutional trap

abstract: Trade frictions are reshaping the adjustment paths of export-oriented food sectors, yet evidence on how they affect industrial resilience remains limited. This study examines the impact of China-US trade frictions on the resilience of the shrimp industry in China’s coastal provinces using panel data on China’s shrimp exports at the six-digit HS code level from 2015 to 2023. Treating the trade friction episode as a quasi-natural experiment, the study applies a continuous difference-in-differences approach based on pre-shock US market dependence to identify the causal effect of the shock. The results show that shrimp industry resilience in coastal provinces followed an overall upward trend during the study period, despite fluctuations, with a notable turning point in 2019 when interprovincial disparities widened. The estimates further show that China-US trade frictions had a significant positive effect on shrimp industry resilience. Mechanism analysis indicates that this effect operated through two complementary pathways: industrial agglomeration (IT) and technological innovation (STI). Specifically, trade frictions significantly promoted the spatial clustering of shrimp value-chain activities and technological innovation, both of which partially mediated the resilience-enhancing effect with Bootstrap-confirmed significance. These findings show that trade shocks do not only disrupt exports. They also induce adaptive restructuring within shrimp-sector value chains, with implications for shrimp resilience, coastal development, and trade policy under rising global uncertainty.
